statement: H1: the gender gap in entrepreneurial activity (nascent or established business ownership) is larger in institutional contexts that mitigate work-family conflict through (a) moderate paid leave for mothers, (b) generous state childcare spending and/or (c) availability of part-time work.
direction: interaction-sign description: negative Female x institution interactions (gap widens with supportive institutions); for paid leave a curvilinear (moderate-length) pattern
estimand: Cross-level interaction coefficients Paid leave x Female, Paid leave squared x Female, Childcare x Female, Part-time employment x Female in Model 3 (three-level mixed-effects logit)
population: Employed adults aged over 18 and under 55 in 24 high-income countries, GEM APS 2001-2008 (143 country-year surveys)

support.row: Institutional effects on the gender gap (4 rows)

notes: Umbrella claim; the component-specific results are C02-C04.

statement: Greater public expenditure on childcare is associated with a significantly larger gender gap in the odds of entrepreneurial activity, net of individual- and country-level controls (supports H1b).
estimand: Coefficient of Childcare x Female in Model 3
notes: Article states that women's probability falls from about two-thirds of men's at zero childcare spending to about half at the highest spending (MAIN p.21).

statement: The estimated effects of paid leave (linear and squared) on the gender gap in entrepreneurial activity are negative but small and not significant.
direction: null-effect (point estimates negative for linear term)
estimand: Coefficients of Paid leave x Female and Paid leave squared x Female in Model 3

support.row: Paid leave x Female; Paid leave squared x Female

notes: Reported as a non-significant result for H1a.

statement: The size of the women's part-time labour force is not significantly associated with the gender gap in entrepreneurial activity.
estimand: Coefficient of Part-time employment x Female in Model 3
notes: Non-significant result for H1c.

statement: Across the whole sample women are just over half as likely as men to be engaged in entrepreneurial activity (strong negative gender effect; men's odds about 1.8 times women's).
estimand: Coefficient of Female in Model 1 (and Models 2-3)
notes: Baseline gender gap; not a numbered hypothesis but a central stated finding.

statement: Middle-aged individuals and those with a postsecondary degree are more likely to be entrepreneurs (age positive, age squared negative, postsecondary positive).
estimand: Coefficients of Age, Age squared, Postsecondary degree in Model 1

support.row: Age; Age squared; Postsecondary degree or higher

statement: Entrepreneurship is less common in countries with higher GDP and much more common where respondents agree that entrepreneurship is a socially valued (high-status) activity; a one-SD higher status score implies about 1.2 times the odds.
estimand: Coefficients of GDP and Social status of entrepreneurship in Model 2 (and Model 3)
scale: log-odds (text converts status effect to odds ratio)
notes: Country-level predictors are standardized, so coefficients are per SD.

statement: Adding the country-level variables (Model 2) explains about 44 percent of the between-country variance in entrepreneurial activity rates (change in between-country intercept SD from Model 1 to Model 2).
estimand: Proportional change in squared between-country intercept SD between Model 1 and Model 2

statement: Including the gender x institution interactions reduces unexplained between-country variance in the gender effect by about 48 percent, but does not explain survey-level variation in the gender gap.
estimand: Proportional change in squared between-country female SD between Model 2 and Model 3; between-survey female SD unchanged

support.row: Between-country female s.d.; Between-survey female s.d.

statement: A likelihood-ratio test comparing empty models with fixed versus random female slope indicates significant between-group variance in the gender gap; ICCs from the unconditional means model are about 6 percent (survey within country) and 5 percent (country).
estimand: LR test of random female slope in unconditional model; ICCs from unconditional means model
notes: No table; the unconditional models are not printed.

statement: The childcare x female result is similar when predicting nascent entrepreneurship only (about 3 percent of the sample).
estimand: Coefficient of Childcare x Female in Online Appendix Table A3 Model 1 (nascent entrepreneurship outcome)
notes: Distinct outcome (nascent only); treated as robustness per the article's framing, not as an interchangeable specification.

statement: The childcare x female result is robust to including individuals who are not employed (full sample with a 'not employed' control).
estimand: Coefficient of Childcare x Female in Online Appendix Table A3 Model 2 (full sample)
population: All adults 18-54 (employed and not employed) in 24 countries, 2001-2008
notes: S1 note states key findings were similar when employment status was not included as a control.

statement: The childcare x female result is robust to including entrepreneurial perceptions (self-assessed ability, fear of failure) and knowing an entrepreneur; these perception variables themselves predict entrepreneurship in the expected directions.
direction: negative (Childcare x Female); positive (ability, knows entrepreneur); negative (fear of failure)
estimand: Coefficient of Childcare x Female and the three perception coefficients in Online Appendix Table A3 Model 3
population: Employed adults 18-54 in 24 countries, 2001-2008, with perception items observed (random half of non-entrepreneurs 2003-2008)

support.row: Childcare x Female; Self-assessed entrepreneurial ability; Fears business failure; Knows another entrepreneur

notes: Skip pattern in 2003-2008 upwardly biases the share of entrepreneurs in this subsample (MAIN p.11 fn 5).

statement: H2: among established business owners, women's relative odds of being motivated by limited employment options are significantly lower in countries with high childcare spending.
estimand: Coefficient of Childcare x Female in Model 4
notes: Predicted probability for women about 9 points lower at highest versus lowest childcare spending (.24 vs .33), MAIN p.24.

statement: H2: women owners' relative odds of being motivated by limited employment options are significantly lower in countries with high rates of women's part-time work.
estimand: Coefficient of Part-time employment x Female in Model 4
notes: About 4 points lower (.27 vs .31) at highest vs lowest part-time rate, MAIN p.24; gap reverses sign at high values.

statement: Paid leave (linear and squared) is not significantly associated with the gender gap in Plan-B motivation among business owners.
estimand: Coefficients of Paid leave x Female and Paid leave squared x Female in Model 4

support.row: Paid leave x Female; Paid leave squared x Female

notes: Not discussed in text beyond the table; inferred from the article singling out childcare and part-time work.

statement: Among business owners, being motivated by limited employment options is more common among older, less-educated, sole owners with older businesses, and in contexts with lower GDP, higher unemployment, fewer women managers and stronger cultural support for entrepreneurship.
direction: positive (age, sole owner, business age, unemployment, social status); negative (postsecondary, GDP, percent women managers)
estimand: Control coefficients in Model 4

support.row: Age; Postsecondary; Sole owner; Business age; GDP; Unemployment rate; Social status; Percent women managers

statement: H3 (business size): the gender gap in business size is unrelated to childcare or part-time work but is significantly smaller in countries providing longer (moderate) paid leave; the gap is smallest at about 25-30 weeks of FTE paid leave and the effect levels off or reverses at very long leaves.
direction: interaction-sign description: Paid leave x Female positive, Paid leave squared x Female negative; childcare and part-time interactions null
estimand: Coefficients of Paid leave x Female, Paid leave squared x Female, Childcare x Female, Part-time x Female in Model 5 (three-level linear mixed model of log business size)

support.row: Paid leave x Female; Paid leave squared x Female; Childcare x Female; Part-time employment x Female

notes: Model 5 is the only linear model in the article.

statement: H3 (growth aspirations): women are significantly less likely to express high-growth aspirations, but the gender gap is significantly smaller in contexts with moderate lengths of paid leave (positive linear, negative squared interaction).
direction: negative (Female); Paid leave x Female positive, Paid leave squared x Female negative
estimand: Coefficients of Female, Paid leave x Female and Paid leave squared x Female in Model 6

support.row: Female; Paid leave x Female; Paid leave squared x Female

notes: Women in contexts with 20-30 weeks of paid leave are described as considerably more likely to express high-growth expectations.

statement: H3 (innovativeness): women's relative odds of offering a product or service that is new to all customers are higher in countries with a moderate amount of paid leave (strong curvilinear interaction); the gap is virtually nonexistent at 20-30 weeks of paid leave.
direction: negative (Female); Paid leave x Female positive, Paid leave squared x Female negative
estimand: Coefficients of Female, Paid leave x Female and Paid leave squared x Female in Model 7
population: Established business owners in 24 countries, surveys 2002-2008

support.row: Female; Paid leave x Female; Paid leave squared x Female

notes: Outcome available only 2002-2008 (Table 2 note; MAIN p.15 fn 14).

statement: H3 (new technology): women's relative odds of using new technology are somewhat higher in countries that generously fund childcare; the interaction is small relative to its SE (marginal), and the gender gap is indiscernible above about 0.4 percent of GDP on childcare.
estimand: Coefficients of Female and Childcare x Female in Model 8
population: Established business owners in 23 countries (Poland excluded), surveys 2005-2008
notes: Outcome available only 2005-2008; Poland excluded (Table 2 note).

statement: Women business owners run smaller businesses, have lower high-growth aspirations, and are less likely to introduce new products or use new technology than men (negative Female main effects in Models 5-8); the Female main effect in the motivation model is small and positive (marginal).
estimand: Coefficient of Female in Models 4-8 (at mean of standardized institution variables)
population: Established business owners in 24 (23 for Model 8) countries
notes: Because institution variables are standardized and interacted, Female is the gap at mean institutional values.

statement: Overall conclusion for H3: models 5-8 offer convergent support that women's representation in growth-oriented entrepreneurship is relatively higher where work-family institutions (moderate paid leave; childcare) mitigate work-family conflict; part-time work is not associated with growth-oriented outcomes.
estimand: Pattern across the gender x institution interactions in Models 5-8
notes: Summary claim; the article notes the pattern differs by outcome (paid leave for size, aspirations, innovation; childcare for technology) and calls it unexpected (MAIN p.29).

statement: Descriptive: aggregate entrepreneurial activity rates range from about 6 percent (France) to about 25 percent (Greece); women are underrepresented in every country and their share bears little relation to the aggregate rate.
estimand: Country-level percentage of the workforce engaged in entrepreneurial activity, by gender
notes: Women's shares cited: France about 36, Belgium 35, New Zealand 46, Greece 35 percent.

statement: Descriptive: country-specific logistic regressions (adjusting for education, age, survey year) give the largest adjusted gender gaps in Ireland, Iceland and Norway (men at least 10 points higher; Ireland men 0.24 vs women 0.11) and the smallest (under 3 points) in Canada, Spain and Japan.
estimand: Average marginal effect of gender on the probability of entrepreneurial activity from separate per-country logits

statement: Descriptive: country-level gender gaps in the probability of entrepreneurship correlate positively with childcare provision (r = .40), weakly with paid leave (r = .14) and not with women's part-time work (r = -.02).
estimand: Pearson correlations between country-level AME gender gaps and country-mean institution measures (24 countries)

statement: The three work-family indicators are not strongly correlated (r = .22, -.30, -.25; Cronbach's alpha .3552; factor loadings below |.49|), so an aggregated index would be inappropriate; pooled VIFs for country-level variables are at most 3.07.
estimand: Correlations, alpha and VIFs among survey-level predictors

statement: Robustness (not shown): results are very similar when policy changes are lagged two years or not lagged; with alternative economic/legal controls (business start-up index, union density, service-sector size); with alternative women's-status indicators; entering macro predictors one at a time; estimating odds ratios; dropping countries with regional heterogeneity; and adding business size as a covariate in Models 6-8.
estimand: Unreported alternative specifications described in footnotes
population: As in the corresponding main models
notes: No tables; cannot be sealed as targets.

statement: Robustness (not shown): in women-only subsamples, women are significantly less likely to be Plan-B motivated where childcare spending is more generous, and there is a significant curvilinear effect of paid leave on women's business size, growth aspirations and new product introduction.
estimand: Institution main effects in women-only models (not tabulated)

statement: Descriptive sample facts: 13 percent of the analytic sample are entrepreneurs; 31 percent of established owners report limited employment options as motivation; 17 percent have high-growth aspirations; 22 percent use new technology; 9 percent introduce a brand-new product or service.
estimand: Sample means

support.row: Entrepreneur; Motivated by limited employment options; High Growth Aspirations; Product/service is new to all customers; Product/service requires new technologies

notes: Comparison material only; S1 Table A1 country-level means are likewise documentary.

statement: In the established-owner models, state childcare spending has a marginal negative main effect on business size and growth aspirations, and GDP has a negative main effect on new technology use.
estimand: Main-effect coefficients of State childcare spending (Models 5, 6) and GDP (Model 8)
notes: Not discussed in text; listed because starred in the table.
